newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian parliament overrules veto on trophy art.
newsitem.headline: Russian parliament overrules veto on trophy art.

text.p: Russia's Federation Council upper house of parliament on Wednesday overruled a presidential veto on a bill asserting Moscow's ownership to art seized from Germany at the end of World War Two.
The results of a postal ballot on the issue showed that 144 deputies in the upper house had voted to confirm the bill, well above the 119 needed to overrule a veto.
President Boris Yeltsin must sign the bill into law in the next seven days, or challenge it in the Constitutional Court.
Alexander Kotenkov, Yeltsin's representative in the upper house which comprises Russian regional leaders, said the chances were better than even that Yeltsin would appeal to the court.
"I expect the possibility of such a decision by the head of the state is more than 50 percent, but the final decision is up to the president," Interfax news agency quoted Kotenkov as saying.
The art, including a priceless Gutenberg bible and paintings by impressionists Claude Monet and Henri Matisse, was seized by the Soviet Red Army from museums and private homes in Germany.
Germany, Russia's biggest Western trading partner, wants the masterpieces back.
But many Russians argue they should stay in Russia as compensation for Soviet sufferings during World War Two. About 27 million Soviet citizens were killed in the war.

The Federation Council members who voted against overruling Yeltsin's veto said this step could have much wider negative impact on Russia then just Germany's displeasure with Moscow's reluctance to return the art.
"We need such a law but some of its articles contradict international agreements Russia has signed before," Konstantin Titov, government of Samara region, told reporters after the voting.

Interfax news agency quoted Deputy Culture Minister Mikhail Shvydkoi as saying the introduction of the law would harm Moscow's newly-aquired democratic image and damage its relations with Western countries.
"This law may bring more harm than benefits," Shvydkoi said.
Some of the opponents of the law suggested that the law, adopted in violation of Moscow's other international committments, was harmful for Russian democracy as well.
"The Council members themslves are closing the door for Russia to develop in a normal and democratic way," said president of the ethnic republic of Tatarstan Mentimer Shaimiyev.
Shaimiyev said that the current generation of Russians, who still have painful memories of World War Two, could hardly have an unbiased judgement on the problem.
"We should have left the law to the next generation," he said.
